blocks.text: **Traversing** an array means visiting its elements one by one. It's the single most common thing you'll do with an array, and there are only a handful of shapes a traversal can take. Learn them once and you'll recognise them in every solution.

blocks.alt: Four ways to walk an array. Forward: from index 0 to the end. Backward: from the end to index 0. Two ends: one pointer from each end, meeting in the middle. All pairs: for each i, j runs over the elements after it.

blocks.text: The classic loop. Use it when you need the **position** as well as the value — to compare neighbours, to write to another array, or to report where something is.
Notice the condition is `i < length`, not `i <= length`. The last valid index is `length - 1`, and `<=` would step one past it — the most common array bug there is.
When you only need the values — summing, counting, finding the max — the "for each" loop is shorter and leaves no index to get wrong.

blocks.code:
let total = 0;
for (const x of nums) total += x;

int total = 0;
for (int x : nums) total += x;

int total = 0;
for (int x : nums) total += x;

blocks.text: Start at the last index and count down to 0. Useful when later elements must be handled first — filling an array from the back, as in **Merge sorted arrays in place**, or building "everything to my right" information.

blocks.code:
for i in range(len(nums) - 1, -1, -1):
    print(nums[i])

blocks.text: In C++, `nums.size()` is **unsigned**. Counting down with an unsigned index never goes below zero — it wraps around to a huge number and the loop never ends. Cast to `int` first, as above.
Put one index at each end and move them toward each other. This is the heart of the **two pointer** technique: reversing, checking palindromes, and finding pairs in sorted arrays all use it.

blocks.code:
left, right = 0, len(nums) - 1
while left < right:
    # look at nums[left] and nums[right] together
    left += 1
    right -= 1

blocks.text: Two nested loops, with the inner one starting just after the outer one, visit every pair `(i, j)` with `i < j` exactly once. That's how most **brute force** solutions look — and why they cost **O(n²)**.
Here is the two-ends traversal reversing an array in place. Step through it and watch the pointers close in; try an odd length and an even length.

items: Need every value, but not the position? **For each**.
Need the position, or to look at neighbours? **Forward with an index**.
Later elements decide earlier ones, or you're writing from the back? **Backward**.
Comparing or swapping from both ends, or searching a sorted array for a pair? **Two ends**.
Every pair, just to get a correct answer first? **Nested loops** — then look for something faster.
